# Patterns serve the flow {#sec-patterns}

A presentation pattern is useful when it makes state changes easier to follow. It is not a
badge to apply to every class.

## MVVM gives a view a model {#sec-mvvm}

Use a view model when a screen needs commands and derived state. QML binds to that model and
does not know where its data comes from. Sketchbook's list view model opens, creates, renames,
and deletes sketches.

The view model exposes the state the screen needs, rather than asking the view to inspect
storage or domain objects. It can then be tested without instantiating the screen. MVC makes
a different split between a model, view, and controller; the names matter less than where
state and decisions actually live.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    V[View: QML] -- commands --> VM[View model: C++]
    VM -. properties and signals .-> V
    VM -- reads and writes --> M[Model and storage]
```

Sketchbook's view model exposes the sketch list and the open name as state. The page calls
commands such as `create()` and `rename()`; validation and storage stay behind those commands.
A Qt Test can construct the view model, call a command, and inspect the resulting model without
loading QML.

## A notification center shares feedback {#sec-notification-flow}

A user needs feedback when an action succeeds, fails, or needs a decision. Without a shared
place for that feedback, each screen must decide where to show messages and what to do when
several arrive at once. A notification center gives the application one place to present them.

This is useful when C++ performs work on behalf of different screens. The code that detects
an event can post a message without reaching into a QML object. The view can then show brief
feedback without interrupting the user, or ask for a decision when the work cannot continue
without one. Use notifications for events that matter to the user; routine background work
usually needs no message.

Sketchbook uses `app::notify::NotificationCenter` for feedback from C++. For example, moving
through the drawing history posts a short message:

::: {.snippet source="src/sketchbook/SketchbookViewModel.cpp"}

```cpp
    connect(&m_canvas, &canvas::CanvasStore::historyMoved
    });\n    m_storage.list();
```

:::

A shared center is helpful when messages come from several features or need consistent
presentation. A simple label or dialog can be enough when feedback belongs to one screen.

## Flux makes edits explicit {#sec-flux}

Use Flux when a stateful editor benefits from one direction of change: a view dispatches an
action, a store produces new state, and the view observes it. Undo and redo fit this model
naturally because the store owns history.

The canvas view sends editing commands to the store. For an edit, the store reduces an action
into a new sketch state and notifies its observers. Undo and redo instead move through the
stored history. Flux is a useful fit here, not a requirement for every screen.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    V[View] -- action --> S[Store]
    S -- state and action --> R[Reducer]
    R -- next state --> S
    S -. changed .-> V
```

Sketchbook represents actions with `std::variant`. Its reducer receives a sketch value and an
action, then returns the next sketch. The store keeps snapshots and moves an index through them
for undo and redo. A new edit after undo discards the redo branch; immutable strokes let the
snapshots share the point data instead of copying every stroke. The history has a size limit.

The reducer handles the different action types in one place. It receives a sketch by value,
applies the action to that copy, and returns the result:

::: {.snippet source="src/canvas/Sketch.hpp"}

```cpp
[[nodiscard]] inline Sketch reduce(Sketch sketch, const Action &action)
    return sketch;\n}
```

:::

`std::visit` selects the handler for the action held in the variant. For example, `AddStroke`
appends a stroke to the copied sketch, while `Clear` removes its strokes. The function returns
that next state without modifying the stored snapshot.

The store decides whether the resulting state belongs in history. A new edit drops states
after the current position, so redo no longer leads to a discarded branch:

::: {.snippet source="src/canvas/CanvasStore.cpp"}

```cpp
void CanvasStore::dispatch(const Action &action)
    moveTo(m_history.size() - 1);\n}
```

:::

The equality check skips edits that make no change. `resize()` drops the redo branch,
`push_back()` saves the new state, and `moveTo()` selects it and notifies observers. The size
check removes the oldest snapshot when the history reaches its limit.

Undo does not create another action or reverse a stroke. It moves to the previous snapshot;
`moveTo()` updates the current position and emits the notifications views and storage need.

::: {.snippet source="src/canvas/CanvasStore.cpp"}

```cpp
void CanvasStore::undo()
        Q_EMIT historyMoved(false);\n    }\n}
```

:::

## Choose the smallest pattern {#sec-choosing}

A simple form may need only a QObject with properties. Add a view model when it clarifies a
screen. Add a store when explicit actions and history pay for themselves. The pattern should
remove decisions from the view, not create another layer of naming.

| Feature | A useful starting point | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Lists, forms, settings | MVVM | Properties and commands map naturally to controls. |
| An editor with history | Flux | Explicit edits and snapshots make undo easier to reason about. |
| A display-only component | QML with required properties | It may not need a separate state object. |

These are tradeoffs, not rules. Keeping snapshots uses memory, and a large document may need a
different history representation. Mixing patterns by feature is fine: Sketchbook uses MVVM
for its list and Flux for the canvas.

**Template:** `src/canvas/CanvasStore.hpp` and `src/sketchbook/SketchbookViewModel.hpp`
